standard.title: Purpose and audience of texts
standard.description: identify the purpose and audience of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students describe similarities and differences between imaginative, informative and persuasive texts (AC9E1LY03). They have not yet identified specific intended audiences and distinguished these from general purposes.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify the purpose and audience of imaginative, informative and persuasive texts.

nodes.label: Identifying text purpose
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the purpose of a given text — to entertain, to inform, to persuade — and connect this to the type of text.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the purpose of one imaginative, one informative and one persuasive text.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and discuss the purposes of a range of texts across all three types, including texts by First Nations Australian authors, explaining what the purpose is and what text features signal it.
wider: Identify texts written by First Nations Australian authors and discuss their purposes — noting where purposes may include preserving cultural knowledge, sharing stories of Country, or engaging with specific communities
Identify advertisements and signs as persuasive texts and discuss what they are trying to persuade the audience to do or believe
success_criteria: Student correctly identifies the purpose of an imaginative, an informative and a persuasive text.
Student can name at least one text feature that signals the purpose of each text.

nodes.label: Identifying intended audience
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the intended audience of a text and explain how they know — using features such as vocabulary, illustrations, form and content as evidence.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the intended audience of a given text and name one feature that indicates this.
nodes.typical_width: Identify intended audiences across several texts — different age groups, community members, consumers — and discuss how text features (vocabulary level, illustrations, context) signal who the audience is.
wider: Compare the audiences for two versions of similar information aimed at different groups (e.g. a children's and an adult's book on the same topic) and identify what features change
Identify the audience for an advertisement or sign and discuss what the creator assumed about that audience

response_modes.reason: Students often think 'audience' means 'people' in a general sense. The concept of a specific, designed-for audience — and the features that mark it — only becomes clear across multiple examples with different audiences. More varied audience examples, not more explanation of one, is the productive move.

success_criteria: Student can identify the intended audience of a text.
Student can name at least one text feature that signals who the intended audience is.
